title: Understanding the Structural Origins of Checkerboard Contrast in Low-Leakage SrHfO3 via 4D-STEM
content: As semiconductor devices continue to scale down, further reductions in gate oxide thickness necessitate the development of high-k dielectrics to minimize leakage current while keeping device reliability during switching. Among high-k dielectrics, HfO2 has been widely studied due to its favorable combination of a large bandgap, high dielectric constant, and compatibility with silicon. However, pure HfO2 films often suffer from a thick low-k interfacial layer, unstable threshold voltage, and high leakage current densities [1]. To address these challenges, various elements have been incorporated into HfO2 films, leading to materials such as Hf1-xTixO, and BaHf1-xTixO3, which exhibit a leakage current of 10-5 A cm-2 [1, 2] and 10-4 A cm-2 at 2 MV cm-1 [3], respectively. In a recent study, SrHfO3 (SHO) which exhibits excellent interfacial quality and large bandgap, has demonstrated an exceptionally low leakage current (10-8 A cm-2 at 2 MV cm-1) while maintaining a competitive dielectric constant (κ = 32) partially due to its large bandgap (∼6 eV) [4–6].
